The embattled chancellor, however, pushed back against any speculation he could have to step down and vowed to press on with reforms

BERLIN — Germany’s increasingly embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz conceded that a key regional election on Sunday was a “disaster” as exit polls suggested the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party was on course for its second win in two weeks.

He pushed back, however, against increasing speculation that he would have to step down and vowed to push through his reform agenda as chancellor with “backbone, steadfastness, and patience.”

An exit poll on the ARD broadcaster put the AfD’s vote in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania at 37% — just ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party on 35.5%.  The AfD’s national co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, called the initial Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result a “sensation.”

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party is facing a dire set of results in state elections, exit polls show, and is set to be squeezed both by the surging far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and parties on the left.

The AfD is projected to win the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on 38%, the exit poll from Germany’s public broadcaster shows, just two weeks after the party had its best result yet in Saxony-Anhalt.

Merz’s CDU is currently on 5%, barely enough to seal representation in the largely rural state, piling pressure on his beleaguered leadership.

In the other election on Sunday, the left-wing Die Linke party leads in Berlin on 26%, followed by the CDU and the Greens, according to the exit polls.

Watch: Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calls for immediate action on fuel costs

Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.
